pages.title: M365 Setup & File Organization Guide
pages.html:
Grade Band B (Grades 6–8) scaffold. This page is pinned in every module so a scholar who enrolls mid-year can find it without asking the teacher.

1 · How to Sign In

Go to office.com and sign in with your school Microsoft account (not a personal Microsoft account). Your username is your Optima email address. If you don't know your password, contact your teacher.

2 · This Course's OneDrive Folder

Create (or confirm you already have) this folder path in OneDrive: Optima → Civics → Civics_2026-27. Save every Word or PowerPoint file for this course there.

3 · File Naming Rule

Every file you submit follows this pattern: LastName_FirstName_AssignmentShortName_CIV8_2627

Example: Reed_Patrick_LockeAnalysis_CIV8_2627. Multi-draft assignments add _Draft1, _Draft2, or _Final.

4 · How to Submit via Canvas

Open the assignment in Canvas. If it uses the OneDrive cloud-assignment tool, your personal copy opens automatically; complete it and click Submit in Canvas when done. If it's a file-upload assignment, use the OneDrive tab in the submission window to attach your saved file directly; don't download-then-reupload.

I Joined Mid-Year: What Do I Do?

  1. Confirm you have a school M365 account. If not, contact your teacher.
  2. Create your Optima → Civics → Civics_2026-27 OneDrive folder if it doesn't exist yet.
  3. Review the file naming rule above and bookmark this page.
  4. Ask your teacher whether any earlier assignments need to be made up in M365 format.

Where to Get Help

Ask your teacher first. For Microsoft's own beginner tutorials, visit support.microsoft.com.

assignments.title: Critical Questions
assignments.html:
MODULE 4 · CRITICAL QUESTIONS
Critical Questions
10 points · written answers
❦ ❧ ❦
Instructions

Open the primary source page Preamble to the Bill of Rights & First Amendment (1791) and read it. Then answer both questions below. Type your answers in the text box, numbering them 1 and 2.

Reread the Preamble/1st Amendment excerpt above, then read it in the context of the lesson “The Price of Ratification” before answering.

  1. The amendment restrains "Congress," not citizens or private businesses. What does this tell you about the difference between a constitutional right and a general moral or social expectation of tolerance?
  2. Suppose the First Amendment had been written to say "No person shall abridge" freedom of speech, rather than "Congress shall make no law" abridging it. Based on this passage, what kind of dispute would this change make newly possible under the First Amendment that is not possible under the actual text?

assignments.title: Primary Source Report
assignments.html:
MODULE 4 · PRIMARY SOURCE REPORT
Primary Source Report
25 points · Word document
❦ ❧ ❦
Instructions

Open the two primary source pages, Preamble to the Bill of Rights & First Amendment (1791) and Second Amendment (1791), and read them both. Then write your report.

Write a short Word document (250-400 words total) answering the following. Quote directly from both primary sources at least once each, and include a Works Cited list.

  1. Both the First and Second Amendments limit what "Congress" or "government" may do, rather than granting citizens something new. Using both primary sources this week, explain in one or two sentences what this shared structure suggests about the framers' underlying theory of where rights come from.
  2. Suppose the Second Amendment had been written without its opening militia clause, reading simply "the right of the people to keep and bear Arms shall not be infringed." Would this change make the individual-rights interpretation easier or harder to argue against? Explain your reasoning.
M365 Reminder

M365 Reminder. Name your file LastName_FirstName_PSReport12_CIV8_2627, save to Optima -> Civics -> Civics_2026-27, and submit through the Canvas OneDrive tab. Include a Works Cited list for both sources.

assignments.title: Critical Questions
assignments.html:
MODULE 4 · CRITICAL QUESTIONS
Critical Questions
10 points · written answers
❦ ❧ ❦
Instructions

Open the primary source page Lemon v. Kurtzman, 403 U.S. 602 (1971) and read it. Then answer both questions below. Type your answers in the text box, numbering them 1 and 2.

Reread the Lemon v. Kurtzman excerpt above, then read it in the context of the lesson “A Test for the Establishment Clause” before answering.

  1. The passage says close government monitoring of religious schools could create the very "entangling church-state relationships... the Religion Clauses sought to avoid." Explain the apparent paradox here: how can trying to enforce separation of church and state end up entangling the two more closely?
  2. Suppose Pennsylvania's law had funded only playground equipment and school lunches at religious schools, with no funding tied to teacher salaries or classroom instruction. Using the Lemon test's three prongs, would you expect this version of the law to survive review? Explain your reasoning.

assignments.title: Primary Source Report
assignments.html:
MODULE 4 · PRIMARY SOURCE REPORT
Primary Source Report
25 points · Word document
❦ ❧ ❦
Instructions

Open the two primary source pages, Lemon v. Kurtzman, 403 U.S. 602 (1971) and Sherbert v. Verner, 374 U.S. 398 (1963), and read them both. Then write your report.

Write a short Word document (250-400 words total) answering the following. Quote directly from both primary sources at least once each, and include a Works Cited list.

  1. Both cases interpret the same sixteen words of the First Amendment's religion clauses, yet apply completely different tests. What does this tell you about the relationship between a short constitutional text and the body of case law that eventually surrounds it?
  2. Suppose South Carolina had denied unemployment benefits to everyone who refused any day of work for any personal reason, religious or not, applying the rule equally to all claimants. Using the Court's reasoning in Sherbert, would this version of the policy likely survive a free exercise challenge? Explain.
M365 Reminder

assignments.title: Critical Questions
assignments.html:
MODULE 4 · CRITICAL QUESTIONS
Critical Questions
10 points · written answers
❦ ❧ ❦
Instructions

Open the primary source page Miranda v. Arizona, 384 U.S. 436 (1966) and read it. Then answer both questions below. Type your answers in the text box, numbering them 1 and 2.

Reread the Miranda excerpt above, then read it in the context of the lesson “The Right to Remain Silent” before answering.

  1. The Court requires "procedural safeguards" before a confession from custodial interrogation can be used, rather than simply asking afterward whether the confession seems true. What does this suggest about whether the Fifth Amendment is more concerned with the reliability of a confession or with how it was obtained?
  2. Suppose Miranda had been read all four warnings clearly at the start of his interrogation but still confessed. Based on this passage, would his confession then be usable against him at trial? Explain your reasoning using the text.

MODULE 4 · PRIMARY SOURCE REPORT
Primary Source Report
25 points · Word document
❦ ❧ ❦
Instructions

Open the two primary source pages, Miranda v. Arizona, 384 U.S. 436 (1966) and Terry v. Ohio, 392 U.S. 1 (1968), and read them both. Then write your report.

Write a short Word document (250-400 words total) answering the following. Quote directly from both primary sources at least once each, and include a Works Cited list.

  1. Terry permits a search based on "reasonable suspicion," a lower standard than the "probable cause" ordinarily required for an arrest or full search. Explain in your own words why the Court might allow a lower standard for a brief, limited intrusion than for a more serious one.
  2. Suppose Officer McFadden had searched Terry's pockets for drugs rather than patting down his outer clothing for weapons. Using the passage's language about a "carefully limited search," would this broader search likely still be justified under Terry? Explain.

assignments.title: Critical Questions
assignments.html:
MODULE 4 · CRITICAL QUESTIONS
Critical Questions
10 points · written answers
❦ ❧ ❦
Instructions

Open the primary source page Brown v. Board of Education, 347 U.S. 483 (1954) and read it. Then answer both questions below. Type your answers in the text box, numbering them 1 and 2.

Reread the Brown excerpt above, then read it in the context of the lesson “Inherently Unequal” before answering.

  1. The ruling holds that segregation deprives students of "the equal protection of the laws guaranteed by the Fourteenth Amendment." Explain in your own words how physical separation by race can amount to a denial of legal equality, even when a state claims the separate facilities are the same in quality.
  2. Suppose a state could prove, with verified data, that its segregated schools were truly identical in funding, facilities, and teacher quality. Based on this passage's reasoning about "inherently unequal," would that evidence change the constitutional outcome? Explain why or why not.

Write a short Word document (250-400 words total) answering the following. Quote directly from both primary sources at least once each, and include a Works Cited list.

  1. Comparing both passages, identify the specific factual or logical claim in Plessy that Brown most directly rejects. State it in one sentence.
  2. Suppose no case like Brown had ever reached the Supreme Court, and Plessy had simply remained unchallenged and controlling. Using judicial review from the lesson “The Shortest, Vaguest Branch”, what would this suggest about how much correcting a bad precedent actually depends on someone bringing a new case, rather than the error correcting itself automatically?

quizzes.title: Intro Wrapper
quizzes.description:
MODULE 4 · INTRO WRAPPER
Intro Wrapper
3 questions · survey · one attempt
❦ ❧ ❦
Instructions

Before we start Module 4 (Civil Liberties and Rights), a few quick check-in questions. This is ungraded and untimed; there is no wrong answer.

questions.text: Module 3 studied how the three branches are structured. This module studies what happens when the government's power runs up against an individual's rights. Before reading, write two or three sentences: can you name a right you think should never be limited, under any circumstances? We'll return to this at the end of the module.
Which best describes what you already know about landmark Supreme Court cases like Miranda or Brown v. Board?

answers.text: I've heard the name but don't know the case
I know roughly what it decided
I know the reasoning behind the decision
I could explain the case's lasting effect on the law

questions.text: Every Thursday assignment this module is a Tier 3 Primary Source Report, worth more toward your grade than a typical week. Do you have a plan for pacing four report weeks in a row?

answers.text: Yes
I'd like a suggested schedule from my teacher

quizzes.title: Reading Quiz
quizzes.description:
MODULE 4 · READING QUIZ
Reading Quiz
5 questions · 5 points · one attempt
❦ ❧ ❦
Before you start

Five inference questions on the Bill of Rights and the First Amendment.

Open the lesson The Price of Ratification first and read it through. Then choose the one best answer for each question below.

questions.text: Based on the lesson, why were the Anti-Federalists unwilling to ratify the Constitution without a promise of amendments?

answers.text: They wanted a monarchy instead
They had already written their own Constitution
They feared the new government's powers weren't clearly enough limited without a written list of protected rights
They opposed having a Congress at all

questions.text: Hamilton's original worry about a bill of rights, according to the lesson, was that it might:

answers.text: Cost too much to print
Give Congress too little power
Imply that any right not specifically listed was unprotected
Make the Constitution too short

questions.text: The lesson describes a bill of rights as 'a fence' rather than 'a grant.' What is the difference between these two ideas?

answers.text: A fence applies only to state governments
A fence marks territory government may not enter; a grant would imply government is the source of the rights
A fence gives citizens new rights; a grant restrains government
There is no real difference

questions.text: The First Amendment begins 'Congress shall make no law...' Based on the lesson, what does this phrasing tell you about who the amendment directly restrains?

answers.text: State governments only
Private citizens
Foreign governments
The national legislature

questions.text: A student claims the Bill of Rights was part of the original 1787 Constitution presented to the states for ratification. Based on the lesson, is this accurate?

answers.text: No, it was added by the first Congress in 1789 and ratified in 1791, after the Constitution itself
Yes
No, because the Bill of Rights was never actually ratified
Yes, but only the First Amendment was original

quizzes.title: Reading Quiz
quizzes.description:
MODULE 4 · READING QUIZ
Reading Quiz
5 questions · 5 points · one attempt
❦ ❧ ❦
Before you start

Five inference questions on Lemon v. Kurtzman and Sherbert v. Verner.

Open the lesson A Test for the Establishment Clause first and read it through. Then choose the one best answer for each question below.

questions.text: Based on the lesson, the Establishment Clause and the Free Exercise Clause are:

answers.text: The same promise stated twice
Found in two different amendments
Two separate promises within the same sentence of the First Amendment
Only about state, not federal, governments

questions.text: The laws struck down in Lemon v. Kurtzman used state funds to:

answers.text: Ban religious schools entirely
Fund a national church
Build new public schools
Pay religious school teachers' salaries for secular subjects

questions.text: According to the lesson, the third prong of the Lemon test asks whether a government action creates:

answers.text: A financial profit for the state
Excessive government entanglement with religion
A secular purpose
A new religious holiday

questions.text: The lesson describes the Lemon test as 'nowhere written in the Constitution's text.' What does this tell you about where the test actually came from?

answers.text: It was part of the original Bill of Rights
The Supreme Court constructed it to help apply the Establishment Clause to real cases
The President created it by executive order
Congress passed it as a statute

questions.text: A student claims the Supreme Court in Lemon v. Kurtzman ruled that all government aid to religious schools is always unconstitutional under any circumstances. Based on the lesson, is this accurate?

answers.text: Yes
No, the Court created a three-part test to evaluate such aid rather than banning it outright in every case
No, because the Court upheld the laws
Yes, but only in Pennsylvania

quizzes.title: Reading Quiz
quizzes.description:
MODULE 4 · READING QUIZ
Reading Quiz
5 questions · 5 points · one attempt
❦ ❧ ❦
Before you start

Five inference questions on Miranda v. Arizona and Terry v. Ohio.

Open the lesson The Right to Remain Silent first and read it through. Then choose the one best answer for each question below.

questions.text: Based on the lesson, which constitutional protection was the central issue in Miranda v. Arizona?

answers.text: The right against self-incrimination during custodial interrogation
Freedom of the press
The right to bear arms
The right to a jury trial in civil cases

questions.text: According to the lesson, the Supreme Court's ruling in Miranda did more than overturn one conviction; it also:

answers.text: Abolished police interrogations entirely
Eliminated the death penalty
Wrote out a specific warning police must give once a suspect is in custody and before interrogation begins
Required all suspects to have a lawyer present at arrest

questions.text: The lesson compares the Miranda ruling to Lemon v. Kurtzman from last week. What specific similarity does it draw between the two cases?

answers.text: Both dealt with religious schools
Both were decided unanimously
Both concern the Second Amendment
Both involve the Court building a practical procedure to make an existing right effective, not adding new constitutional text

questions.text: Why does the lesson say an unrepresented suspect is in a weaker position than 'the Constitution's text alone can protect'?

answers.text: The Constitution does not apply to accused persons
The Fifth Amendment only applies in civil cases
The pressure of custodial interrogation by trained officers can overwhelm a suspect's awareness of rights that exist only on paper
Police are not bound by the Constitution

questions.text: A student claims Ernesto Miranda was found factually innocent of the crime he was accused of. Based on the lesson, is this accurate?

answers.text: Yes
No: the ruling concerned the constitutionality of how his confession was obtained, not his factual guilt or innocence
Yes, and he was awarded damages
No, because the Court refused to hear his case

quizzes.title: Reading Quiz
quizzes.description:
MODULE 4 · READING QUIZ
Reading Quiz
5 questions · 5 points · one attempt
❦ ❧ ❦
Before you start

Five inference questions on Brown v. Board of Education and Plessy v. Ferguson.

Open the lesson Inherently Unequal first and read it through. Then choose the one best answer for each question below.

questions.text: Based on the lesson, the central constitutional question in Brown v. Board of Education was whether:

answers.text: States could refuse federal funding for schools
Public schools should exist at all
Private schools must admit all students
Racially segregated public schools could ever actually satisfy the Fourteenth Amendment's equal protection guarantee

questions.text: According to the lesson, Chief Justice Warren argued that segregated schools harmed black children:

answers.text: Only when teachers were less qualified
Regardless of whether resources were formally equal, because separation itself communicated inferiority
Only if the physical buildings were in worse condition
Only in Southern states

questions.text: The lesson notes the Brown ruling was decided by a vote of:

answers.text: 5 to 4
6 to 3
The case was never actually decided
All nine Justices, unanimously

questions.text: Based on the lesson, did the Brown ruling immediately desegregate schools the following day?

answers.text: Yes, but only in Kansas
No, because the ruling was reversed shortly after
No: enforcement required years of further litigation and federal action
Yes, instantly and completely

questions.text: A student claims the 'separate but equal' doctrine originated with the Brown decision itself. Based on the lesson, is this accurate?

answers.text: Yes
No, because 'separate but equal' was never actually a real legal doctrine
No: 'separate but equal' existed for nearly sixty years before Brown, which overturned it
Yes, and it was struck down the same year

quizzes.title: Outro Wrapper
quizzes.description:
MODULE 4 · OUTRO WRAPPER
Outro Wrapper
5 questions · survey · one attempt
❦ ❧ ❦
Instructions

Now that we're finishing Module 4 (Civil Liberties and Rights), a few reflection questions before we move into Module 5. This is ungraded and untimed; there is no wrong answer.

questions.text: Revisit your answer from the Module 4 Intro Wrapper: a right you thought should never be limited. After studying the Bill of Rights and four landmark cases, would you still describe that right as absolute, or has your answer become more conditional? Explain.

How confident do you feel explaining the difference between a constitutional right stated in the Bill of Rights and the specific legal test (such as the Lemon test, the Sherbert test, or the Miranda warnings) courts built later to apply it? (1 = not at all confident, 5 = very confident)
Of the four Primary Source Reports this module, which case's reasoning did you find most difficult to follow?

answers.text: Bill of Rights (1st & 2nd Amendments)
Lemon v. Kurtzman & Sherbert v. Verner
Miranda v. Arizona & Terry v. Ohio
Plessy v. Ferguson & Brown v. Board of Education

questions.text: What is still unclear to you after Module 4?

answers.text: answer

questions.text: Justice Harlan dissented alone in Plessy v. Ferguson in 1896, holding a position the full Court would not adopt for fifty-eight years. Name one virtue (courage, courtesy, honesty, perseverance, self-government, service, responsibility) this required of him, and explain in a sentence why.

answers.text: answer
